segments.text: Hi, come on in and have a seat. I have the letter from your physiotherapist here, from your last visit, and she mentions that your shoulder was getting better. What's happened since then?
Yeah, it was getting better, I was really pleased. But then on Saturday my shoulder is acting up again, and this time it's a whole different kind of thing.
A different kind of thing. Can you describe it for me, in your own words?
Kind of a dull zing, deep inside, and when I try to reach for a shelf it just kind of gives out. Like the arm isn't hooked up properly.
So a deep dull ache, and the arm gives out when you reach up. When did this begin, exactly?
Three days ago. I was lifting a box of books off the top shelf in the garage, and I felt something go. Not a crack, more like a rubber band snapping.
Something went, like a rubber band, three days ago, when lifting a box overhead. Did it hurt right at that moment?
It sort of took my breath away for a second, and then I carried on, because I figured it would walk itself off. It didn't.
That's very understandable. What makes it worse, and does anything help?
Anything over my head makes it worse, like putting a shirt on or reaching up for a coffee mug. Resting it against my side is the only thing that helps.
Overhead movements are the trigger, and resting it against your side eases it. Okay. Are you taking anything for it?
Just ibuprofen, 400 mg, about every six hours when it's bad. It takes the edge off, but not all the way.
Ibuprofen 400 mg, as needed. Fine. Any numbness or tingling in your arm or hand, or anything with your nerves?
No, nothing like that. My hand feels totally normal.
Good to hear. Let me ask about your past health. Anything ongoing, like diabetes or blood pressure?
Yeah, I have type 2 diabetes, about seven years now, and high blood pressure too. Both pretty well controlled.
Type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, noted. Any surgeries in the past?
I had my gallbladder out, about eight years ago. That's the only one.
Thanks. Now let me have the nurse read me your numbers, and then I'll check the shoulder.
Sure. Blood pressure is 134/82, pulse 76 bpm, temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 %. All taken about ten minutes ago.
Thank you, those are fine. Okay, I'm going to move your arm gently. Tell me when it zings.
There. Right there, that's the zing.
Now, try lifting the arm out to the side by yourself, as high as you can, while I hold your elbow.
It's stuck about here, like halfway up, and then it just drops.
You have weakness lifting the arm out to the side past about shoulder height, and it drops when you let go. That's an important finding.
Is that bad? You've got a worried face.

No, this is my thinking face. Let me explain my thinking. The tendon that did well in physio may have been aggravated, and I think the most likely explanation is a partial rotator cuff tear on top of your old problem.
A tear? Like, ripped?
A partial one, most likely. But I can't rule out a full-thickness tear yet, and the only way to tell the two apart is to look at the tendon.
So that's why it feels like the arm's not hooked up. Okay, so what do we do?
I'd like to arrange an ultrasound of your shoulder today. The nurse will check whether the scan room is free.
The ultrasound room has a gap in about twenty minutes, doctor. I can walk him down.
Twenty minutes, great. I'll just sit in the waiting area and read the magazine about boats.
And if the ultrasound isn't clear enough, we might consider an MRI, but let's see what the ultrasound shows first.
Okay. So ultrasound now, maybe an MRI later. Do I keep the sling thing?
Keep the arm close to your side for now, avoid lifting anything overhead, and keep taking the ibuprofen the way you have been.
No more garage shelves for a while. Got it.
Exactly. And if the pain gets much worse, or the arm gets weaker over the next few days, call us and we'll get you back in right away.
Okay, I will. Thanks for seeing me so quickly, doctor.
Of course. Go with the nurse now, and try not to worry.
